population.note: FICTIONAL ESTIMATES. These figures count current use of any incretin for any reason, so they read slightly higher than Gallup's 2026 weight-loss-only figure. Current use rose only 0.5 pp in two years, but the users changed a lot. Ever-use climbed from 15% to about 23%, so for the first time more US adults are former users (~11.5%) than current ones. About 48% of ever-users have stopped and restarted at least once. One-year persistence improved only a little (~38–40%), mostly among people on orals and the alcohol-use cohort. Starts went up because orals made starting easy: about 45% of new starts in 2028 were pills. Exits went up too: the price barrier stayed, the 2028 blunting label gave people a reason to stop, and status-driven quitting followed the aesthetic inversion. The income gradient flattened and flipped in the middle. The top third fell from an estimated ~14% to ~12% as affluent users quit, cut to low doses, or hid use behind strength training. The middle third (~13%) is now the most medicated, helped by $149–249 cash channels. The bottom third (~9.5%) is still rationed by coverage: only about 22 states joined the Medicaid deal at Medicare rates. The 65+ share rose from 9% to 11% under the extended Medicare Bridge pilot, slowed by prior authorisation and clinicians' worries about muscle loss in older adults. The 50–64 share fell from 22% to 19% as employer coverage drifted down and long-term users cycled off. Under-18 use is ~0.3% of all minors (~220k), mostly adolescents 12+ and still skewed to upper-income families, although those families are also the most likely to talk about their teens going 'unmedicated'. US adult obesity is ~35.0% (36.4% in 2026). The decline is slowing and is now concentrated in the middle-income group.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: the GLP-1 Bridge pilot was extended without redesign through Dec 2029 at the same terms ($245/month to Medicare, ~$50 copay, BMI/comorbidity criteria). Semaglutide's IRA-negotiated Medicare price ($274/month) took effect Jan 2027 for the diabetes/CV labels. Medicaid: about 22 states opted into coverage at the Medicare-equivalent rate; several others capped enrolment or kept exclusions for budget reasons. The VA covers semaglutide for alcohol use disorder with comorbid obesity or T2D under its own updated guideline. No new federal or state mandate.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Generic semaglutide is now routine across ~160 countries, including India ($6–40/month), China (domestic generics since 2026), Brazil and Canada (~CAD 75–110, ~US$55–80). Generic liraglutide is everywhere. Tirzepatide is still under patent almost everywhere. Personal mail-order importation of Canadian generic semaglutide is a known, tolerated grey channel for some tens of thousands of Americans.
access.note: Prices fell along a managed path. Injectable cash prices through TrumpRx and manufacturer direct channels stepped from ~$350 (2026) to $199–249. Oral starting doses held at $149, and maintenance doses run $149–299. The new oral amycretin launched at $299 cash. Retatrutide launched at a ~$999 list price with a $449 direct-cash tier and almost no plan coverage; it sets the high end. List prices for legacy brands were trimmed toward ~$999, but almost nobody pays list. Employer coverage drifted from 60% to ~57%. There was no structural change, just continued tightening of BMI thresholds, step-therapy-to-oral requirements and prior authorisation. In 2027 the FDA finalised the exclusion of semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide from the 503B bulks list. Compounding shrank to residual 503A volume. Telehealth now mostly resells branded product through manufacturer direct channels, which is the route the 'calm' programmes use. By volume, weekly injectables are ~60% of current users and orals ~40%, but orals are ~45% of new starts.

on_market_classes: GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1/amylin combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema, approved early 2027; modest uptake after losing head-to-head vs tirzepatide)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, approved Jun 2028)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill 25 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1/amylin single-molecule co-agonist, daily oral (oral amycretin, approved Sep 2028; ~20% at 72 weeks, non-inferior to tirzepatide 15 mg head-to-head)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: alcohol use disorder with comorbid obesity or type 2 diabetes. This is guideline-endorsed only (ASAM and VA/DoD updates Nov 2027, APA practice guideline 2028), not an FDA indication: a semaglutide sNDA for AUD is under review with a decision expected 2029
mainstream_offlabel_uses: low-dose 'craving management' / 'calm' programmes sold by telehealth to people without obesity, using branded orals at starting doses ($149) and marketed around focus and freedom from 'noise'
alcohol use disorder without obesity: the guideline does not cover it, but the prescribing happens anyway, often cash-pay
nicotine, cannabis and sports-betting compulsions, with observational support and one small positive smoking-cessation RCT
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
misuse by people with restrictive eating disorders, using cheap orals as appetite suppressants
drugs.pipeline_note: The field has split along the reward axis. One camp is developing brain-sparing, peripherally restricted agonists marketed as 'weight loss without the flattening'; the first phase 2 data are expected 2029. The other is pushing CNS-active incretins as addiction drugs: semaglutide AUD phase 3, plus phase 2 programmes in smoking and gambling disorder. MariTide (monthly injectable) phase 3 readouts are expected 2029. Subcutaneous amycretin phase 3 is ongoing. Muscle-preserving adjuncts (bimagrumab combinations) are in phase 3, and their marketing now borrows the 'strength' language of the aesthetic inversion. Retatrutide's dysesthesia and the class blunting label are why its uptake is slow despite 28% efficacy. Consensus 2030 global incretin-market forecasts were cut from ~$150–162B to ~$120–130B because US net prices fell and US current-use plateaued, even as global volume rose.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common class effect and the leading cause of discontinuation, concentrated at initiation and dose escalation. Orals show similar rates, and the oral peptides add the burden of fasting before each dose.
Elevated with rapid weight loss; higher absolute numbers at retatrutide-level efficacy.
No causal link confirmed in extended outcome trials; absolute risk low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; mass-tort litigation ongoing, with no bellwether verdict for plaintiffs yet.

safety_ledger.effect: Lean mass (muscle) loss and bone density
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ~25–40% of weight lost is lean mass, depending on population and drug. Bone-density decline is confirmed in older users in two cohort studies. Concern has moved from clinics into culture and now feeds the strength-training ideal.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change; geriatric society guidance (2027) recommends resistance training and protein targets alongside therapy. Muscle-preserving adjuncts are in phase 3.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Evidence still conflicts. A large 2027 multinational cohort found a small elevated risk (~1.3×) concentrated in people with diabetes.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label retained; FDA added it to postmarketing adverse reactions (2027) without a boxed or class warning.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association across regulators and reviews. Some confusion with the new blunting label persists in public discussion.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Warning removed (2026); FDA clarified in the 2028 labelling that blunting is distinct from depression or suicidality.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: The 2028 class label states that clinically meaningful decreased interest or pleasure occurred in ~4% of patients vs ~1.5% on placebo. This comes from a pooled post hoc analysis of ~19,000 trial participants re-scored with retrospective patient-reported items, plus a prospective postmarketing study using the Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale. The effect is dose-related (~6–7% at the highest triple-agonist doses) and resolves within 4–8 weeks of dose reduction or discontinuation in most patients. In real-world user surveys, 12–18% report some subjective flattening, and this gap between the label figure and lived experience is unresolved.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA class labelling change (Feb 2028) under Adverse Reactions and Patient Information. EMA labelled it in 2027. No boxed warning. Postmarketing requirement for prospective measurement in adolescents.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Real-world data now converge on partial regain, roughly 40–60% of lost weight within a year off-drug, with faster regain after injectable-to-nothing than after taper-to-oral. Because so many people cycle, it is the most widely shared experience of the drugs.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; payers increasingly require step-down to oral maintenance rather than stopping coverage outright.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Iron, B12, vitamin D and protein insufficiency confirmed in long-term users with very low intake. Most common in older adults and low-dose 'calm' users who are not under dietitian care.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Professional-society screening recommendations (2027); no label change.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; adolescents on therapy for decades; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About six years of rigorous follow-up now exist. Nearly half of ever-users have cycled at least once, and no trial has studied cycling as an exposure. The first adolescent cohorts are entering their twenties.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements on each new approval; an NIH-funded cycling cohort was announced 2028 and will not report before 2032.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit product harms (dosing errors, contamination)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Reports declined after the 2027 503B exclusion. Residual harms now come mainly from counterfeit 'oral' products sold online and from mislabelled imported vials.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503B exclusion finalised 2027; continued warning letters; CBP seizures of counterfeit tablets.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Reported in roughly 1 in 10 patients at higher doses in phase 3, mostly mild and transient.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled at retatrutide approval (Jun 2028); dose-titration guidance.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ED clinicians report rising presentations involving cheap low-dose orals obtained through cash telehealth with minimal screening; not yet quantified.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None federally; two professional societies issued screening guidance for telehealth prescribers (2028).

food_and_beverage.state: About 25% of US households now include a GLP-1 user, fewer than 2026 projections because adoption plateaued. Snack, confectionery and sugary-drink volumes keep falling ~1–2% a year, and protein remains the dominant callout. The aesthetic inversion opened a second lane: 'full-fat', 'real food' and indulgence premium lines are pitched at unmedicated, muscle-building consumers, so some brands now market both portion-controlled 'GLP-1 friendly' SKUs and 'eat big' protein-dense SKUs. JPMorgan-style revenue-loss estimates for 2030 were trimmed toward the low end (~$30B).

alcohol.state: Still contracting. The 2027 AUD guideline endorsement put the drugs directly in front of the heaviest drinkers, who are the industry's profit base: the top 10% of drinkers account for ~60% of volume. US spirits depletions are down mid-single digits for a second straight year. Diageo and Brown-Forman have cut US workforce and SKUs and lean on non-alcoholic and premium 'occasion' products, which so far do not offset the volume loss. Sports-betting operators have started citing GLP-1 adoption as a factor in softening per-customer handle.

restaurants.state: Bifurcated but stable. Quick-service has lost snack and side attachment and sells smaller, protein-heavy formats. The high end benefits from the inversion: abundance menus, family-style plates and 'come hungry' marketing have returned as status signals, and conspicuous eating in public is fashionable among the affluent. Overall traffic is roughly flat.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists stabilised at a smaller base after store closures. The re-buying wave at smaller sizes is over. The new growth is in cuts for muscled bodies (broader shoulders, larger thighs) and in strength-training apparel, with brands quietly widening the fit of their 'athletic' lines.

fitness.state: The fastest-growing consumer category the drugs touched. Strength gyms, hypertrophy coaching and recovery services are growing double digits. The 'GLP-1 companion' programmes of 2026 have been rebranded around strength and 'unmedicated vitality', even though many of their clients are on low doses.

insurance.state: No structural change. Pharmacy trend moderated from ~11.5% to ~8–9% as unit prices fell. GLP-1s remain ~12% of claims where covered. Plans increasingly require step-down to oral or lower-cost agents and won't cover retatrutide or the new oral amycretin at launch. AUD-only claims are mostly denied outside the VA, which pushes those patients to cash.

pharma.state: Global volume is growing fast on ex-US generics and branded orals, while US net price per prescription is down ~30% since 2026 and US current-use is flat, so US revenue is roughly level. Lilly still leads, now with retatrutide. Novo's oral amycretin approval (Sep 2028) is its first credible comeback product. More than 800 GLP-1R programmes are in development, and investor attention has shifted to the reward axis (brain-sparing vs addiction-targeted).

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: A thin body now reads as medicated and cheap, something that can be had for $149 a month. In national surveys ~41% of adults say a thin stranger is 'probably on medication', and the phrase is not admiring. The scarce body is visibly muscled and visibly hungry: lifting four mornings a week, eating a full plate in public, and making a point of being 'unmedicated'. Muscle signals time, coaching, protein budgets and recovery, which a pill cannot supply.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The gradient flipped. Affluent people use 'unmedicated' as a credential, though many quietly keep low doses running under the strength routine. The middle third is now the most medicated and has the thinness the affluent have abandoned. The bottom third is the least medicated, still rationed by coverage, and has the highest obesity. It is judged from both sides at once: fat in a culture that thinks fat is optional, and unable to afford the time-intensive muscled body that replaced thin as the status ideal. Adolescents from upper-income families are both the most likely to be prescribed and the most likely to perform refusal.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Smaller portions remain normal in medicated households. Among the affluent, eating has become a visible performance again: tasting menus, family-style feasts, 'second helpings' in social media posts. Appetite is shown off much as restraint once was. Mixed dinner tables, with one person medicated and one not, are a common source of quiet friction.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: The largest dating app added an optional 'unmedicated' badge in 2028, and it is worn disproportionately by urban professionals under 40. Being 'on it' is something people disclose or are asked about on early dates, partly because of appearance and partly because the blunting label made it a question about desire. Some couples negotiate dose changes around anniversaries and holidays.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite has moved from symptom to status. It is pharmacological territory and a regulated adverse-effect category, but in public culture it has become a sign of vitality and of being fully present. 'Food noise' is still common language, now with a counter-phrase: 'I like the noise.'

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: The FDA label (Feb 2028) puts clinically meaningful blunting at ~4% vs ~1.5% placebo, dose-related and mostly reversible. In user surveys 12–18% report some subjective flattening. A third, unmeasured group of 'calm' programme customers, estimated at 1–1.5 million US adults, take low doses in part because they want the effect.
interior_life.framing: The same effect is now described in four ways. The label calls it an adverse effect ('decreased interest or pleasure'). Addiction medicine calls it a treatment mechanism (the 2027 AUD guidelines). Telehealth sells it as a feature: 'quiet', 'steady', 'no noise', and the ads never use the word anhedonia. Critics and the unmedicated treat it as a character question: are you choosing to want less? FDA letters can police specific claims but not the lifestyle framing.
interior_life.effect_on_work: There is no employer policy, but there is a visible productivity subculture. Sales, trading, software and shift-work forums trade dose schedules for 'focus without the 3 p.m. snack spiral'. Some lifestyle-spending accounts reimburse cash telehealth by default. Counter-anecdotes describe lost ambition and flat performance reviews. Two small observational studies show no net productivity difference. Managers have learned not to ask.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: 'Unmedicated' has become a credential among musicians, comedians and writers, and several have publicly gone off before tours or books, citing the label. Low-dose users report less binge-watching, gaming and betting, and operators notice. High-intensity sensory products (sour, spicy, loud, cold-plunge) are a recognisable niche among medicated consumers chasing a signal.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Reduced libido and emotional distance now appear in the patient leaflet, which made them discussable. Couples therapists report 'dose conversations' as a new standard topic. Some partners describe the medicated person as easier to live with, and others as absent. Some medicated people time drug holidays around relationships, which adds to cycling.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: No measurable effect on turnout or voting. Rhetorically, the drugs split the governing coalition: the administration's price deals are a populist talking point, while the MAHA wing calls the 'calm' programmes 'Big Pharma selling sedation'. On the left there are op-eds about a 'medicated workforce'. Neither line has become legislation.

state.regulatory_posture: Still pro-access and pro-speed. Retatrutide and oral amycretin were approved on priority timelines, and the Bridge pilot was extended. The posture is paired with enforcement on marketing rather than access: a class blunting label, untitled and warning letters to telehealth platforms over explicit mood or productivity claims, and the compounding exclusion finalised. FDA has not tried to restrict low-dose prescribing to people without obesity, which is legal off-label.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No new action. Medicare Bridge extended unchanged through 2029. The IRA negotiated price for semaglutide is in force. Medicaid participation is voluntary state by state. Nothing is mandated.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Unchanged: BMI/comorbidity criteria, prior authorisation, and step-to-oral requirements that tightened inside existing rules. No adherence monitoring or benefit conditioning beyond standard utilisation management.
state.workforce_or_military: No policy. The VA prescribes GLP-1s for alcohol use disorder heavily under its 2027 clinical guideline. This is clinical practice, not workforce policy, though veterans' groups track it.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: The US-abroad price gap persists and is widely known: ~$199–299 at home versus ~$55–80 in Canada and under $40 in India. Indian and Chinese generic makers are scaling exports to ~160 countries, and Novo and Lilly compete abroad on price and at home on next-generation molecules. Personal importation from Canada is tolerated rather than authorised. US exclusivity still runs to ~2031–32, and the coming patent cliff is starting to shape 2029–30 pricing strategy.

events.event: Medicare's negotiated price for semaglutide ($274/month) takes effect; TrumpRx and manufacturer direct channels step injectable cash prices to $199–249 while holding oral starting doses at $149

ASAM and the VA/DoD update alcohol use disorder guidelines to recommend semaglutide for patients with comorbid obesity or type 2 diabetes; Novo files a supplemental application for AUD; private insurers say they will not cover AUD-only use without an FDA label

FDA adds emotional blunting to GLP-1 class labelling: clinically meaningful loss of pleasure in about 4% of patients vs 1.5% on placebo, dose-related and usually reversible; manufacturers say benefit-risk is unchanged

Major telehealth platforms launch low-dose oral 'calm' subscriptions at $149/month promising 'no noise'; FDA issues untitled letters over focus and mood claims, and the platforms revise the copy but keep the programmes

Gallup: 11.5% of US adults currently on an incretin, 23% ever, with former users outnumbering current users for the first time; 41% say a thin stranger is 'probably on medication'; the largest dating app's new 'unmedicated' badge is adopted by millions in its first month

FDA approves Novo Nordisk's oral amycretin, a daily pill non-inferior to injectable tirzepatide at ~20% weight loss over 72 weeks; it launches at $299 cash, and most plans place it behind step therapy

open_tensions: Blunting is on the label at ~4% and in ads as 'quiet'. Users report flattening at three to four times the label rate, and a million-plus people take low doses partly to get it. The line between adverse effect and product is now being drawn by ad copy, and the FDA hasn't decided whether to draw it differently.

Oral parity has removed the needle barrier but not the price or coverage barrier. The 2029 question is whether a $299 pill expands use or just speeds up churn among people already cycling, and whether payers' step-to-oral rules become a quiet way to ration.

Nearly half of ever-users have cycled on and off, and the first adolescent cohorts are reaching adulthood. There are no data on what years of intermittent dampening of appetite and reward do to bodies or temperaments, and the NIH cohort won't report until 2032.

The status ideal has moved from thin to muscled and hungry, which costs time and money a pill can't supply. The bottom third is still the least medicated and most obese and is now judged from both directions. The Medicare Bridge extension ends in Dec 2029, and the patent cliff is visible from 2031.

prose.headline: Thin Is Cheap Now: The Pill That Made Slimness Ordinary and Turned Appetite Into the Last Status Symbol
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028 the share of American adults on an incretin drug has barely moved. It is about 11.5 percent, half a point higher than two years ago, and that stillness is the most misleading number in the country. Underneath it the population has turned over. Nearly a quarter of adults have now used one of these drugs, and more Americans are former users than current ones. Roughly half of everyone who ever started has stopped and come back at least once. The pills made starting easy. Nothing made staying easy.

Prices fell as far as the negotiators promised and no further. Medicare pays $245 a month under a Bridge pilot that was quietly extended to 2029, and semaglutide's negotiated Medicare price took effect in 2027. Cash prices through manufacturer and TrumpRx channels sit between $149 and $299. The share of employers covering weight management has drifted down to about 57 percent. Across the border generic semaglutide costs about sixty dollars a month in Canada and less than lunch in India, and Americans know it.

The needle no longer stops anyone. Pills were already close to half of new starts when, in September, the FDA approved Novo Nordisk's oral amycretin. It is a daily tablet that matched injectable tirzepatide head to head at about twenty percent weight loss. It launches at $299 cash into the same coverage system as everything else, and most plans put it behind step therapy. Lilly's retatrutide, an injection reaching twenty-eight percent, arrived in June at a premium almost no plan covers.

Two decisions changed what the drugs mean. In late 2027 addiction-medicine guidelines and the VA endorsed semaglutide for alcohol use disorder in patients with obesity or diabetes. In February 2028 the FDA added emotional blunting to the class label: a clinically meaningful loss of pleasure in about four percent of patients, against one and a half on placebo, dose-related and usually reversible. The label was meant as a warning, but people read it as a list of what the drug does. Within months telehealth platforms were selling low-dose oral subscriptions that promise quiet: no food noise, no third drink, no midnight scrolling. The ads never use the word anhedonia. The FDA can object to a sentence in an ad. It can't object to a mood.

Meanwhile thinness stopped signalling much of anything. A slim body that can be had for $149 a month no longer says discipline or money, and the people who used it to say those things have moved on. The prestige body now is visibly muscled and visibly hungry. Its owner lifts four mornings a week, eats a full plate in public and mentions being unmedicated. The largest dating app offers that as a badge. Strength gyms are the fastest-growing part of fitness, and expensive restaurants are selling abundance again.

So the user base is changing shape. The top income third has drifted down as the affluent quit, or hide low doses behind their trainers. The middle third is now the most medicated. The bottom third, still rationed by coverage, is the least medicated and the most obese, and is judged from both sides at once. Food companies have adapted to smaller appetites with protein and to the new ideal with full-fat lines. Alcohol keeps shrinking as its heaviest customers are treated out of drinking. Pharma volume grows abroad while US net prices fall.

Nothing has collapsed, and nobody has been made to take anything. Instead a molecule that turns down wanting is both a warning on a label and a product in an ad. Millions of people are setting the dose of their own capacity for pleasure, raising it and lowering it as they go, with no decade of data on what that does.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Tanya Brandt's alarm goes at 5:50, half an hour before she's allowed coffee. She swallows the small white tablet with four ounces of water, as the app insists, and stands at the kitchen window while the half hour passes. That half hour used to be the worst part of her day. Now no part of the day is the worst part.

At the claims office in Dayton, Kenzie from the next pod has a new sweatshirt that says FED in block letters. Kenzie eats a breakfast burrito at her desk with a kind of ceremony. Tanya eats four almonds and closes forty-one files before lunch, a personal record. She feels about it the way she feels about the weather.

At noon she reads the leaflet again, the folded one she keeps behind her library card. May cause decreased interest or pleasure in usual activities. About 4 in 100 people. She has decided she is not one of the four. She has also stopped going to Thursday trivia, but that's because the bar changed owners.

When she gets home her daughter Ava, sixteen, is at the stove cooking six eggs and talking about her deadlift. The thin girls at school, Ava says, look rented. Mike comes in from the garage. He went off Zepbound when the plant dropped coverage, got about half of it back, and doesn't talk about it.

The pinot grigio from Easter is still in the fridge door. She notices it the way you notice a coat left behind by someone who moved out.

At ten she checks the alarm: 5:50. She could skip one. She doesn't.
